sections.body: Zhang distinguishes the treaty baseline rules from an argument based on custom, compiles examples of national practice, and argues for a treatment of outlying archipelagos that goes beyond the express archipelagic-state rule. sections.heading: 2. Argument and evidence by section
sections.body:
**UNCLOS Articles 7 and 47 address different baseline regimes.** Articles 46 and 47 frame archipelagic baselines for an archipelagic State. Article 7 addresses distinct coastal circumstances. This confirms the treaty structure; the proposed customary extension requires its own argument.

**Custom is analyzed through practice and acceptance as law.** Article 38(1)(b) of the ICJ Statute identifies international custom as evidence of a general practice accepted as law. A catalog of baseline claims establishes only part of the customary-law inquiry.

**The UK statutory example is a 1989 order.** The UK legislation register identifies the instrument as made and confirms the date and title. Its role here is one example of a State instrument, whose generalizability calls for separate analysis.

**The 2016 tribunal’s Spratly analysis supplies a different legal assessment.** The tribunal concluded in 2016 that the Spratly Islands cannot generate maritime zones collectively as a unit and did not accept a distinct regime for those features. Its award followed the article and did not determine territorial sovereignty. The author’s broader historical practice claim remains interpretive.
